title: Multi-Region Topologies
summary: Active-passive, active-active, read-local/write-global, and follow-the-sun are the four concrete shapes a multi-region system takes — each buying a different guarantee for a different cost.

slides.markdown:
Once you've decided a system needs to be multi-region (previous topic), you still have to pick a **shape** — and "multi-region" isn't one architecture, it's a family of them.

This topic covers the four shapes that actually get built: **active-passive** (a standby that takes over), **active-active** (every region serves live traffic), **read-local/write-global** (read nearby, write to one owner), and **follow-the-sun** (the write owner moves with the working day). Each trades consistency guarantees against operational complexity differently.

slides.sectionTitle: Active-passive: a warm standby that takes over on failure
slides.markdown:
In **active-passive**, one region — the primary — serves all live traffic while a second region continuously replicates data but serves nothing until a failover is triggered. The passive region is "warm": provisioned and up to date, but idle.

This is the simplest multi-region shape to reason about: at any moment, exactly one region owns writes and reads, so there's no cross-region conflict to resolve. The cost is that the passive region's capacity sits unused day-to-day, and failover itself — promoting the passive region, redirecting traffic — takes real time, typically minutes.

Active-passive is the right default when you need survival against a regional outage but don't need every region serving traffic simultaneously.

slides.sectionTitle: Active-active: every region serves live reads and writes
slides.markdown:
In **active-active**, two or more regions simultaneously accept both reads and writes from real users — there's no idle standby, every region is doing production work all the time. Losing one region just means the others keep serving; no failover promotion step is needed.

The cost is what active-passive avoids entirely: two regions can now accept conflicting writes to the same record at nearly the same time, so the system needs a real conflict-resolution strategy — last-write-wins, CRDTs, or application-level merge logic — and eventual consistency between regions becomes a fact you design around, not an edge case.

Active-active earns its complexity when you need every region's capacity used continuously and can tolerate, or design around, eventual cross-region consistency.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: active-passive failover vs active-active traffic split
slides.markdown:
![Active-passive fails a dead primary over to a promoted standby, while active-active splits live traffic across two regions linked by bidirectional replication](assets/active-passive-vs-active-active.svg)

Active-passive's diagram has a single "before" and "after" moment — traffic moves wholesale when the primary dies. Active-active's diagram has no such moment: both regions are always live, and the interesting part is the replication arrow between them, which is where conflicts get created and resolved.

That replication arrow is the tell in an interview sketch: if it's one-directional, you're describing active-passive; bidirectional, active-active.

slides.sectionTitle: Read-local, write-global: reading nearby, writing through one owner
slides.markdown:
**Read-local, write-global** is a middle ground: every region can serve reads from its own local replica — fast, no cross-region hop — but all writes funnel through a single owning region, which is the source of truth.

This avoids active-active's conflict problem entirely, since only one region ever accepts a write for a given piece of data, while still giving distant users fast reads most of the time. The cost shows up on the write path: a user far from the write-owning region pays the full cross-region latency on every write, and if the write-owning region goes down, writes stop everywhere until failover completes, even though reads keep working.

This shape fits read-heavy workloads with a tolerable write-side latency hit — a global content platform where reads vastly outnumber writes is the classic case.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-the-sun: the active write region shifts with the working day
slides.markdown:
**Follow-the-sun** is a variant of single-write-owner where the owning region deliberately moves on a schedule — writes are served from Asia during Asian business hours, then handed to Europe, then the US, tracking where the bulk of active users currently are.

It keeps the single-writer simplicity of read-local/write-global while giving the region actually generating most write traffic the low-latency local write path, at the cost of a scheduled handover process that has to run correctly every single day without dropping in-flight writes.

This shape suits systems with a strong regional usage pattern tied to time of day — enterprise tools used mostly during business hours in each region — rather than services with continuous, evenly spread global traffic.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: the four topologies by consistency, cost, and failover complexity
slides.markdown:
| Topology | Consistency | Steady-state cost | Failover complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active-passive | Strong (single writer) | Standby capacity mostly idle | Promotion step, minutes |
| Active-active | Eventual, needs conflict resolution | Full use of every region | None needed — others already live |
| Read-local, write-global | Strong (single writer) | Reads cheap everywhere, writes cross-region for most users | Writes stall until owner fails over |
| Follow-the-sun | Strong (single writer, scheduled) | Local writes for the current active region only | Scheduled handover, plus unplanned failover risk |

**How to decide:** if you can tolerate eventual consistency and need every region's write capacity used, go active-active; otherwise pick a single-writer shape and choose which flavor by whether your traffic is latency-sensitive on writes (read-local/write-global) or has a strong daily regional pattern (follow-the-sun). Consistency guarantees across these shapes are exactly the trade-offs a consistency-model discussion covers in the abstract — here they're driven by which region is allowed to write when.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: calling it active-active when every write still serializes through one region
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We serve reads from three regions, so we're active-active."

**Why it's wrong:** active-active specifically means every region accepts writes, not just reads. A system where three regions read locally but all writes still funnel through one owning region is read-local/write-global wearing an active-active label — it doesn't have active-active's conflict-resolution burden, but it also doesn't have active-active's write availability: if the one write-owning region goes down, the whole system stops accepting writes even though the other two "active" regions are still up.

**Correct model:** ask specifically where writes for a given record are accepted, not where reads are served. If the answer is "one region, always," you have a single-writer topology regardless of how many regions serve reads — say so precisely, since the failure mode is different.
